content: This review is part of a series of Cochrane reviews that investigate various methods of pain management during childbirth. It specifically focuses on the effectiveness and safety of hypnosis for managing pain during labour and childbirth. The review updates a previous version and follows a standardized protocol shared across the series. The authors searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group’s Trials Register up to September 30, 2015, as well as reference lists of primary studies and review articles. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared hypnosis (used either as preparation for labour or during labour itself) with placebo, no treatment, or other pharmacological or non-pharmacological pain relief methods. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed the quality of the trials, contacting study authors when additional information was needed. Nine trials involving a total of 2,954 women were included in the review. The quality of the trials varied, with some being well-designed and others providing limited information about their methodology. Eight of the nine trials assessed antenatal hypnotherapy, but there were significant differences in the timing and techniques used. One trial focused on hypnotherapy administered during labour. The review compared hypnosis interventions with all control groups combined, as well as with specific control conditions such as standard care, supportive counselling, and relaxation training. In the main comparison, women in the hypnosis group were less likely to use pharmacological pain relief or analgesia compared to those in the control groups (average risk ratio [RR] 0.73, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.57 to 0.94, based on eight studies involving 2,916 women; very low-quality evidence). However, there were no clear differences between the hypnosis and control groups for most other primary outcomes. For example, there was no significant difference in women’s sense of coping with labour (mean difference [MD] 0.22, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.58, based on one study involving 420 women; low-quality evidence) or in the likelihood of spontaneous vaginal birth (average RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.32, based on six studies involving 2,361 women; low-quality evidence). Regarding satisfaction with pain relief, no clear differences were observed between the hypnosis group and control groups for women who received pethidine (MD 0.41, 95% CI -0.45 to 1.27; one study, 72 women), Entonox (MD 0.19, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.57; one study, 357 women), self-hypnosis (MD 0.28, 95% CI -0.32 to 0.88; one study, 160 women), or epidural (MD -0.03, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.34; one study, 127 women). A slight benefit in favour of hypnosis was noted for women who used water immersion (MD 0.52, 95% CI 0.04 to 1.00; one study, 174 women; all low-quality evidence). Similarly, no clear differences were found when satisfaction with pain relief was measured as the number of women reporting adequate pain relief (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.20, based on one study involving 264 women; low-quality evidence). It is important to note that for outcomes such as pharmacological pain relief and spontaneous vaginal birth, there was significant statistical heterogeneity, which could not be fully explained through subgroup analysis. For secondary outcomes, no clear differences were observed between the hypnosis and control groups for most measures. Evidence regarding pain intensity, satisfaction with the childbirth experience, and postnatal depression was mixed. Data from multiple trials were available for these outcomes but could not be combined due to differences in measurement methods. One small study suggested that fewer women in the hypnosis group stayed in the hospital for more than two days after giving birth (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.83), but no clear differences were found for other secondary outcomes. When comparing hypnosis with specific control conditions, no clear differences were found between the hypnosis group and the standard care or relaxation training groups for the primary outcomes. However, compared to the supportive counselling group, women in the hypnosis group were less likely to use pharmacological analgesia (average RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.73, based on two studies involving 562 women) and more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth (RR 2.42, 95% CI 1.43 to 4.07), although the latter finding was based on one small study. These comparisons showed less statistical heterogeneity than the main comparison. The authors concluded that there are still relatively few studies assessing the use of hypnosis for labour and childbirth. Hypnosis may reduce the overall use of analgesia during labour, but it does not appear to reduce the use of epidurals. No clear differences were found between the hypnosis and control groups for satisfaction with pain relief, sense of coping with labour, or spontaneous vaginal birth. The evidence for the main comparison was rated as low quality for all primary outcomes due to concerns about inconsistency, design limitations, and imprecision. The authors recommend further research in the form of large, well-designed RCTs to better assess the value of hypnosis for pain management during labour and childbirth.
